                                       My Trusted Source ExxonMobil moves into focus as crude prices retreat following an easing of Middle East tensions over the weekend, spotlighting the integrated major and the forces shaping the US oil and gas sector. ExxonMobil (NYSE:XOM) has moved into the market spotlight as crude prices retreated sharply following an easing of tensions in the Middle East over the weekend, a shift that rippled quickly across the energy sector. The pullback in oil came as fears over disruptions to supply eased, sending both global and US crude benchmarks lower and pressuring the shares of the largest producers. For an integrated major like ExxonMobil, whose fortunes are woven into the global price of oil and gas, such swings are part of the terrain. As the new week opens, the market is weighing what the retreat in crude signals for the sector and how the largest producers are positioned to navigate a backdrop where geopolitics can move prices in a matter of hours. The oil and gas sector sits at the foundation of the global economy, supplying the energy that powers transportation, industry, and daily life. It spans a long chain of activity, from the exploration and production of crude and natural gas, through the refining that turns raw hydrocarbons into usable fuels, to the marketing that delivers those products to customers. Prices across this chain are set in global markets that respond to the balance of supply and demand, and that balance can shift quickly in response to economic conditions, production decisions, and geopolitical events. Because energy is so essential and so widely traded, the sector is unusually sensitive to headlines, and a single development in a distant region can move prices around the world. That sensitivity was on full display over the weekend as an easing of tensions sent crude lower. ExxonMobil is an integrated major, meaning it operates across the entire length of the oil and gas chain rather than focusing on a single segment. Its upstream business explores for and produces crude and natural gas from fields around the world, including a substantial position in the prolific basins of North and South America. Its downstream operations refine crude into fuels and lubricants and market those products to customers. And its chemicals arm turns hydrocarbons into the building blocks of countless everyday products, from packaging to automotive components. The company is also pursuing lower-carbon efforts in areas such as carbon capture and hydrogen. This breadth is the defining feature of the integrated model: when crude prices fall, refining and chemicals can sometimes benefit from cheaper feedstock, providing a measure of balance across the cycle. The largest producers moved through their reporting season having delivered strong results earlier in the year, supported by firm energy prices and disciplined spending. Commentary from the majors emphasized their focus on operating efficiently, keeping costs in check, and distributing capital back to the owners of the business through dividends and capital-distribution programs, all while continuing to spend on their most productive assets. The integrated majors described maintaining their spending plans even as prices fluctuated, a sign of the discipline that has characterized the sector in recent years. That steadiness matters because it allows these companies to weather the swings of the commodity cycle without abandoning the long-term projects that underpin their production, and it has become a central theme in how the majors present themselves to the market. A defining feature of the current backdrop is the outsized role that geopolitics continues to play in energy markets. Tensions in key producing regions can send prices surging on fears of disrupted supply, while a de-escalation can send them tumbling just as quickly, as happened over the weekend. This sensitivity reflects how tightly the global market is balanced, with limited spare capacity to cushion shocks. Alongside geopolitics, the decisions of major producing nations about how much to pump remain a powerful force, shaping the supply side of the equation. And the long-term transition toward cleaner energy continues to influence how the majors allocate capital, balancing their traditional operations against emerging lower-carbon efforts. Together, these developments keep the sector in a state of constant recalibration. The environment for oil and gas is shaped above all by the global balance of supply and demand. On the demand side, the health of the world economy determines how much energy is consumed, with growth lifting consumption and slowdowns tempering it. On the supply side, the production decisions of major exporting nations, the output of US shale fields, and the ever-present possibility of disruption all play a role. Prices sit at the intersection of these forces, and they can move sharply when the balance shifts. The weekend retreat in crude, prompted by an easing of tensions, illustrated how quickly sentiment can turn when a perceived threat to supply recedes. For the integrated majors, navigating this environment means staying disciplined through the swings rather than chasing every move in price. Several currents are reshaping energy, and reporting across US oil and gas stocks has spotlighted them together. Capital discipline has become a hallmark of the sector, with producers favoring steady spending and generous distributions over aggressive expansion. Geopolitics continues to inject volatility, as tensions and their easing swing prices. The long transition toward cleaner energy is prompting the majors to fund lower-carbon efforts alongside their traditional operations. And consolidation has reshaped the competitive map, as larger producers acquire assets to build scale in the most productive basins. Each of these trends is influencing how the integrated majors position themselves for a landscape where the demand for energy remains vast even as its sources gradually evolve. ExxonMobil enters this stretch as one of the largest integrated majors in the world, with operations spanning exploration, refining, chemicals, and emerging lower-carbon efforts. Its scale gives it advantages in cost, technology, and access to major projects, allowing it to compete across the entire energy chain. Its substantial position in prolific producing basins anchors its upstream business, while its refining and chemicals operations provide balance when crude prices swing. And its work in areas such as carbon capture positions it for a landscape where lower-carbon energy is growing in importance. This diversified positioning reflects the enduring logic of the integrated model, which the company emphasizes as a source of resilience through the ups and downs of the commodity cycle. Beyond the swings in crude, recent activity in the sector has centered on the majors' continued discipline in spending and their steady distributions to the owners of the business. The largest producers have described maintaining their spending plans even as prices fluctuate, a sign of the restraint that has defined the sector in recent years. Some have entered into technology licensing agreements and struck deals to add drilling capacity in their most productive fields, reflecting a focus on operating efficiently rather than expanding at any cost. The combination of steady spending, generous distributions, and targeted spending on the best assets sketched a sector determined to weather the commodity cycle with discipline, a theme the market has been keen to understand amid the volatility. At an operational level, the integrated majors are concentrating on efficiency, cost control, and disciplined capital allocation. Efficiency means squeezing more production from their assets while keeping expenses in check, a discipline that has become central to how these companies operate. Cost control matters especially in a business where prices are set by global markets beyond any single company's control, since keeping costs low allows a producer to remain resilient even when prices fall. And disciplined capital allocation means directing spending toward the most productive assets while returning surplus cash to the owners of the business. ExxonMobil has framed much of its operational messaging around these themes, emphasizing the durability that comes from operating efficiently across the entire energy chain through the swings of the cycle. The oil and gas sector faces persistent headwinds. Prices are volatile and set by global forces beyond any company's control, meaning even the best-run producer can see its revenue swing sharply with the market. Geopolitical events can disrupt supply or send prices tumbling with little warning. The long transition toward cleaner energy poses questions about the demand for hydrocarbons over the coming decades, prompting the majors to balance their traditional operations against emerging efforts. And the capital-intensive nature of the business means large sums must be committed to projects that take years to pay off. Managing these crosscurrents is part of the everyday work of running an integrated major, and the market watches closely how each company navigates the swings of the commodity cycle. Competition in oil and gas is intense and spans the globe. The integrated majors compete with one another for access to the best resources, for efficiency in refining, and for scale in chemicals. They also face national oil companies with vast reserves, independent producers focused on particular basins, and a growing field of firms pursuing lower-carbon energy. Scale offers the majors advantages in cost and technology, but it does not insulate them from the swings of the commodity cycle or from the rise of alternative energy sources. ExxonMobil competes across all of these fronts, and the market watches how it defends its position through disciplined operations while balancing its traditional business against the gradual evolution of the global energy mix. The price of crude offers one of the clearest windows into the forces acting on the sector, reflecting in real time the balance between what the world produces and what it consumes. When a threat to supply emerges, prices can surge; when that threat recedes, as it did over the weekend, they can fall just as quickly. For the integrated majors, these swings flow directly into the value of the oil and gas they produce, even as their refining and chemicals operations can provide some balance. The behavior of crude prices, much like the pulse of the consumer for a retailer, serves as a barometer for the health of the sector and for the geopolitical and economic forces shaping the global energy market from one week to the next. Capital discipline has become the defining ethos of the integrated majors, a lesson etched by past cycles when aggressive spending in good times left producers exposed when prices turned. Today the largest producers emphasize steady, measured spending directed toward their most productive assets, alongside generous distributions to the owners of the business. This restraint means resisting the temptation to ramp up sharply when prices rise, and staying steady rather than slashing when they fall. The aim is durability: a producer that spends within its means through the cycle can weather downturns without abandoning the long-term projects that underpin its production. For the integrated majors, whose projects can take years to develop and pay off, this steadiness is especially important. It also reassures the owners of the business, who value the predictability of steady distributions over the boom-and-bust pattern that characterized earlier eras. This discipline has become a central theme in how the majors present themselves and in how the market judges their resilience. Because energy is so essential and so widely traded, the fortunes of the largest producers carry relevance well beyond their own results. As a component of the S&P 500, ExxonMobil features in how the market reads the health of the energy sector, and swings in crude prices ripple across the broader market, influencing everything from transportation costs to inflation expectations. When oil retreats on an easing of tensions, the effect is felt across many industries that depend on energy. When it surges on fears of disruption, that too echoes widely. This is why the movements of crude and the reporting from the major producers draw such close attention, offering a read on the global economy that reaches far beyond the oil and gas sector itself.                                        My Trusted Source ExxonMobil has completed its corporate redomiciliation to Texas, a move landing as firmer crude prices and shipping-route disruptions reshape the backdrop for its upstream operations. ExxonMobil (NYSE:XOM) has completed its corporate redomiciliation to Texas, shifting its state of incorporation away from New Jersey in a move that closes out a process the company had signaled for months. The shift lands at a moment when firmer crude prices and disruptions to global shipping routes used by crude and liquefied-gas carriers are lending support to upstream results across the integrated energy space, giving the redomiciliation added resonance beyond the realm of corporate paperwork. The decision to redomicile is more than a symbolic gesture toward the state where ExxonMobil already maintains its operational headquarters in Spring, a suburb of Houston. Texas has, over recent years, positioned itself as a preferred jurisdiction for corporate charters, offering a specialized business court system and statutes that companies have described as more predictable and less prone to prolonged litigation than those found in some other states. ExxonMobil joins a lengthening roster of large public companies that have opted to reincorporate in Texas, a trend that has picked up pace as boards and general counsel offices weigh the comparative advantages of different legal domiciles. For a company of ExxonMobil's scale, the redomiciliation carries practical implications touching corporate governance, the venue for legal disputes, and the framework under which stockholder meetings and votes are conducted. The company has framed the change as consistent with where its workforce, infrastructure, and decision-making already reside, given that Texas has long served as the operational nerve center for its upstream, downstream, and chemical businesses. The move also arrives against a backdrop in which several other prominent energy and industrial names have made similar transitions, reinforcing the sense that Texas is consolidating its standing as a hub not just for physical energy infrastructure but for corporate charters themselves. The redomiciliation news coincides with a period in which crude benchmarks have firmed, a dynamic that matters enormously for a company whose upstream segment remains the single largest driver of overall results. Crude pricing has been shaped by a mix of factors this year, including supply management by major producing nations, demand patterns tied to industrial activity across large economies, and periodic bouts of geopolitical tension that have injected volatility into tanker movements and shipping lanes. Disruptions affecting vessels that carry crude oil and liquefied natural gas through key maritime corridors have added a layer of support to prices, as market participants price in the added cost and complexity of rerouting cargoes or insuring vessels transiting contested waters. These disruptions have periodically affected chokepoints that matter for global energy flows, prompting shippers to adjust routes, extend voyage times, and in some cases pay materially higher insurance premiums. For an integrated major like ExxonMobil, this environment has generally supported the price realizations achieved across its upstream portfolio, even as the downstream and chemical segments continue to navigate their own separate set of margin dynamics tied to refining spreads and petrochemical demand. ExxonMobil's upstream business spans a global footprint that includes the Permian Basin in West Texas and New Mexico, deepwater developments offshore Guyana, assets in the Gulf of Mexico, and a portfolio of international positions spanning multiple continents. The Permian remains a centerpiece of the company's domestic production strategy, with the company continuing to apply advanced drilling and completion techniques to extract barrels efficiently from unconventional formations. Guyana, meanwhile, has emerged as one of the more closely watched growth stories in the global upstream space, with a series of floating production vessels brought online in recent years that have rapidly scaled output from what was, not long ago, a frontier exploration area. The combination of these legacy and newer assets gives ExxonMobil a production base that is more diversified than many of its integrated peers, spreading exposure across onshore unconventional resources, offshore deepwater fields, and a mix of oil-weighted and gas-weighted output. This diversification has helped the company capture upside when crude prices firm while also providing some insulation when individual basins face localized headwinds, whether from weather events, regulatory changes, or infrastructure bottlenecks. Beyond the upstream segment, ExxonMobil operates an extensive downstream refining network and a global chemical manufacturing business that together provide a counterweight to the cyclicality inherent in crude production. Refining margins have fluctuated through the year as global product demand patterns shift, with gasoline, diesel, and jet fuel consumption all subject to seasonal swings and broader economic currents. The chemical segment, which produces feedstocks and derivatives used across packaging, construction, and consumer goods manufacturing, has faced its own set of pressures tied to global industrial demand and competition from new capacity additions in other regions. The integrated model that spans upstream, downstream, and chemicals has long been a defining characteristic of ExxonMobil's structure, distinguishing it from pure-play exploration and production companies that carry more concentrated exposure to crude price swings. This structure allows the company to smooth some of the volatility that would otherwise flow directly to the bottom line when crude prices move sharply in either direction. ExxonMobil operates in a competitive field that includes Chevron (NYSE:CVX), which also maintains a large-scale integrated model spanning upstream production and downstream refining, as well as European majors and a range of independent exploration and production companies with more concentrated regional footprints. Within the domestic natural gas and liquids export space, companies such as Cheniere Energy (NYSE:LNG) have built distinct positions around liquefied natural gas export infrastructure, a segment that has grown in strategic importance as global buyers look to diversify supply sources. The competitive dynamics among these companies play out across several dimensions, including cost of production, access to low-cost resource basins, downstream integration, and the pace at which each company brings new production online. ExxonMobil's scale advantages, drawn from decades of accumulated infrastructure, technical expertise, and balance sheet capacity, have generally allowed it to pursue large, capital-intensive projects that smaller companies would find difficult to finance or execute. The Guyana development, in particular, illustrates this dynamic, representing a scale of offshore capital deployment that few companies beyond the largest integrated majors could realistically undertake. The broader energy sector has continued to navigate a period defined by several intersecting trends. Global demand for crude oil and refined products has remained resilient even as electrification and efficiency gains slowly reshape long-run consumption patterns in some regions. At the same time, natural gas has taken on a growing role both as a power-generation fuel and as an export commodity, with liquefied natural gas cargoes increasingly bridging supply gaps in regions seeking to diversify away from single-source pipeline dependence. Shipping and logistics disruptions have periodically punctuated this backdrop, adding friction to global energy flows and, in turn, supporting prices for both crude oil and liquefied natural gas. These disruptions have underscored the strategic importance of maritime chokepoints and have prompted renewed attention to the resilience of global energy supply chains. For companies like ExxonMobil that maintain global production and shipping footprints, these dynamics require constant operational recalibration, from adjusting tanker nominations to managing insurance and routing decisions in real time. Regulatory and legal environments across different jurisdictions have also become a more prominent consideration for large energy companies, feeding into decisions such as ExxonMobil's redomiciliation. Companies operating across many states and countries must weigh differing tax treatments, permitting timelines, and litigation exposure when deciding where to locate both physical infrastructure and corporate charters. The trend toward Texas incorporation reflects, in part, a broader reassessment among corporate boards of where the balance of predictability, cost, and legal familiarity best serves long-run operational needs. ExxonMobil has emphasized capital discipline in recent years, favoring a portfolio approach that prioritizes lower-cost, higher-margin projects over volume growth for its own sake. This approach has meant selectively advancing developments in the Permian and Guyana while maintaining more measured spending in higher-cost or less economically attractive basins. The company has also pursued a series of acquisitions and portfolio adjustments designed to concentrate its resource base around assets it considers most competitive on a full-cycle cost basis. This discipline extends to how the company allocates cash generated from operations, balancing reinvestment in production capacity against distributions to stockholders through dividends and buyback programs. The approach reflects a broader shift across the integrated energy space, where companies have generally moved away from the aggressive volume-growth strategies that characterized earlier cycles and toward a framework that emphasizes free cash flow generation and capital efficiency. Several operational themes are likely to remain central to how ExxonMobil is evaluated by market participants and industry watchers in the period ahead. Continued ramp-up of production capacity in Guyana, ongoing efficiency gains in the Permian, and the pace of project execution across the company's global portfolio will all factor into how the upstream segment performs. On the downstream side, refining margins tied to seasonal product demand and the broader health of global industrial activity will shape how that segment contributes to overall results. The chemical business, meanwhile, continues to navigate a period of oversupply in certain regions as new manufacturing capacity has come online globally, pressuring margins for commodity-grade products. ExxonMobil has sought to differentiate its chemical portfolio through specialty and performance products that command steadier margins, a strategy shared by several peers navigating similar industry-wide capacity pressures. The developments surrounding ExxonMobil carry relevance well beyond the company itself, touching on broader themes that resonate across the Energy Stocks category. The interplay between firmer crude prices, shipping-route disruptions, and corporate domicile decisions illustrates how operational, market, and legal considerations increasingly intersect for large energy companies. As a constituent of the NYSE Composite, ExxonMobil's performance and strategic decisions are often read as a proxy for broader sentiment toward the traditional energy complex, even as the sector continues to coexist alongside a growing renewable and lower-carbon power generation landscape led by companies such as NextEra Energy (NYSE:NEE). The redomiciliation itself, while primarily a legal and administrative matter, has drawn attention because of the signal it sends about how large energy companies are thinking about long-run corporate structure at a time when the operating environment for crude and natural gas remains dynamic. Whether other major energy companies follow a similar path in the period ahead remains a topic of ongoing discussion among market watchers tracking corporate governance trends across the sector. ExxonMobil's operational presence in Texas has grown substantially over recent years, anchored by its campus north of Houston that consolidated operations previously spread across multiple sites. The redomiciliation formalizes a relationship between the company and the state that has already been deepening through years of infrastructure spending, workforce expansion, and engagement with local and state governments on matters ranging from permitting to workforce development programs tied to the energy and petrochemical industries concentrated along the Gulf Coast. The Gulf Coast region more broadly continues to serve as a critical hub for energy infrastructure, hosting a dense concentration of refining capacity, petrochemical manufacturing, and export terminals that collectively make the region one of the most significant energy corridors globally. ExxonMobil's decision to formalize its corporate home in Texas reinforces the state's centrality to the broader domestic and global energy supply chain, a positioning shared by numerous other companies with significant Gulf Coast operations. Beyond crude oil, natural gas and liquefied natural gas have taken on outsized importance for the broader energy complex, and ExxonMobil maintains meaningful exposure to both through its upstream gas production and its participation in liquefied natural gas export ventures along the Gulf Coast and in other regions internationally. Disruptions affecting liquefied-gas carriers moving through key maritime corridors have added a layer of complexity to global gas flows this year, prompting buyers in Asia and Europe to adjust sourcing patterns and, in some cases, pay elevated prices for cargoes rerouted around affected chokepoints. This dynamic has reinforced the strategic value of flexible, diversified gas supply, a theme that resonates across companies with liquefied natural gas exposure, including Cheniere Energy (NYSE:LNG), which has built its entire commercial model around long-term export contracts tied to global gas demand. ExxonMobil's own gas positions, spanning both domestic unconventional resources and international liquefaction ventures, place it among the handful of companies capable of supplying meaningful incremental volumes to global buyers seeking to diversify away from single-source pipeline dependence, a priority that has only grown more pronounced amid recurring shipping disruptions. ExxonMobil has continued to emphasize technology as a lever for improving well productivity and lowering per-barrel costs across its unconventional and deepwater portfolios. In the Permian, this has meant longer lateral wells, more precise completion designs, and greater use of data analytics to optimize drilling schedules and reduce non-productive time on rigs. These efficiency gains have become an increasingly important differentiator among operators competing for capital and drilling inventory in a basin that has matured considerably since its early growth years. Offshore in Guyana, technology has manifested differently, with the company deploying advanced subsea architecture and floating production vessels engineered to bring new fields online on accelerated timelines compared with historical deepwater project cycles. The pace at which successive vessels have been sanctioned and brought into service reflects a broader industry shift toward standardized, repeatable project designs that shorten the interval between discovery and first output, a capability that has become a meaningful competitive differentiator in the deepwater segment specifically. ExxonMobil has maintained a long-standing record of returning cash to stockholders through both dividends and buyback programs, a practice the company has continued even through periods of commodity price volatility. This approach reflects a broader capital allocation framework that prioritizes steady distributions alongside disciplined reinvestment in the highest-return segments of the portfolio. The balance between funding growth projects such as Guyana and the Permian on one hand, and maintaining consistent stockholder distributions on the other, has remained a central theme in how the company communicates its capital allocation priorities to the broader market. This framework has also shaped how ExxonMobil approaches acquisitions, favoring transactions that add durable, low-cost resource positions rather than pursuing scale for its own sake. The company's approach in this regard mirrors strategies pursued by Chevron (NYSE:CVX) and other integrated peers, all of which have gravitated toward similar capital discipline principles following a period in prior years marked by heavier spending and, at times, lower capital efficiency across the broader upstream sector. The combination of a sharp move in oil and an imminent earnings print has placed the company squarely in focus, since few names are as closely tied to the direction of crude as this integrated giant. The attention reflects the way ExxonMobil sits at the heart of the energy story running through the market. When oil surges on supply fears, the largest producers become the most direct beneficiaries in the eyes of market participants, and the company's scale across exploration, production and refining makes it a natural reference point. With geopolitics keeping crude volatile, the run-up to its report has taken on added weight this week. The immediate trigger is twofold: crude oil pushing above the hundred-dollar mark on Red Sea disruption and Houthi attacks, and ExxonMobil's scheduled earnings report at week's end. The jump in oil prices lifts the value of every barrel the company produces, while the coming print will show how the business is translating a firmer energy backdrop into results across its upstream and downstream operations. The Red Sea disruption matters because it threatens the smooth flow of crude and refined products through a critical maritime corridor, stoking fears of tighter supply. Those fears feed directly into higher prices, and for a producer of ExxonMobil's magnitude, a sustained move in oil can reshape the earning power of the enterprise. That linkage is precisely why the stock has stepped into sharper focus as the week begins. The oil and gas sector spans exploration and production at one end, midstream transport and storage in the middle, and refining and marketing at the other. ExxonMobil is an integrated major, meaning it operates across this entire chain, from pulling crude out of the ground to turning it into fuels and chemicals supplied to end markets. This integration is a defining feature that distinguishes the largest players from pure-play producers. The sector's fortunes swing with the price of crude, which itself responds to the balance of global supply and demand and to geopolitical events like the current Red Sea tensions. When prices climb, upstream producers capture more value per barrel, though refining margins can compress if crude costs outrun fuel prices. ExxonMobil's spread across the chain gives it a degree of natural balance, cushioning some of the swings that buffet narrower operators. ExxonMobil organizes its business around upstream exploration and production, downstream refining and marketing, and a large chemicals arm. The upstream unit develops oil and gas fields across continents and offshore basins, while the downstream network turns crude into gasoline, diesel and other fuels. The chemicals division converts hydrocarbons into plastics and specialty products used across manufacturing. This integrated structure is central to how the company generates and balances its earnings. When crude prices are high, the upstream segment prospers; when they ease, refining and chemicals can pick up some slack. The company has also pursued a portfolio of large developments in prolific basins, aiming to grow output from low-cost barrels while pruning higher-cost assets. This disciplined shaping of the asset base is a recurring theme in how ExxonMobil describes its strategy. The market environment this week is dominated by two forces for the energy group: the surge in crude and the crowded earnings calendar. While megacap technology names and a Federal Reserve rate decision command attention elsewhere, energy majors are being watched through the lens of the oil move, which touches inflation, corporate earnings and the broader mood of the market. title: Nasdaq Futures Lead US Premarket Rally As Iran Ceasefire Reports Ease Fears Ahead Of Big Tech Earnings: Why NVDA, ORCL, SPCX, XOM, OTLK Are In Focus - Stocktwits
content: U.S. stock futures surged early Monday after reports that the United States and Iran agreed to pause military strikes over the weekend triggered a sharp selloff in crude oil prices. Wall Street gears up for one of the busiest weeks this year, with nearly one-third of S&P 500 companies scheduled to report earnings, including four Magnificent Seven companies: Apple Inc. (AAPL), Amazon.com Inc. (AMZN), Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) and Meta Platforms Inc. (META). Investors will also be watching the Federal Reserve’s July policy decision, second-quarter GDP data and the Fed’s preferred inflation gauge, the PCE price index later this week. As of 4:00 a.m. ET, Nasdaq futures soared 1.5%, Dow and S&P 500 futures rose 0.9%, and Russell 2000 futures were up 1.2%. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment for the SPDR S&P 500 ETF (SPY), an exchange-traded fund that tracks the S&P 500 Index, remained ‘extremely bearish,’ while the Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ), which tracks the Nasdaq-100 Index, has moved to ‘bearish’ from ‘extremely bearish’ last week. Nvidia (NVDA): Rose 1% in early premarket trade after reports revealed it is in talks to provide a $250 billion financing backstop for OpenAI’s 10-gigawatt Ohio data center project. NVDA also announced a $500 billion partnership with SK Group, a $1B investment in South Korea's Naver, and the rollout of its first U.S.-made GB300 chips from TSMC’s Arizona fab. Oracle Corp. (ORCL): Shares saw a 3% relief rally in early premarket trade on Nvidia’s reported $250B OpenAI backstop. Since OpenAI is one of Oracle's largest cloud customers, traders viewed the development as a potential boost to Oracle’s long-term AI infrastructure business. Meanwhile, China's Moonshot AI is reportedly preparing to open-source its Kimi K3 model, renewing debate over whether Chinese AI developers are closing the gap with OpenAI and Anthropic. Alphabet Inc. (GOOGL): In focus after a top executive confirmed memory chip price hikes (up sixfold) will force higher pricing for the upcoming Pixel 11 series. SpaceX (SPCX): Shares were muted early premarket trade ahead of its Aug. 4 earnings report. Morningstar warned that upcoming post-IPO lockup expirations (Aug 6) could create selling pressure while simultaneously boosting the stock's float-adjusted weight inside the QQQ ETF. Outlook Therapeutics (OTLK): Shares rose 7% in early premarket trade following FDA approval of Lytenava for wet age-related macular degeneration (wet AMD), with analysts forecasting up to 290% upside. Oil stocks (USO, BATL, TPET, XOM, CVX, OXY) remained in focus as crude oil prices fell over 6% following the U.S.-Iran military pause. Other tickers trending on Stocktwits at the time of writing included Rigetti Computing (RGTI), Venture Global (VG) and Capricor Therapeutics (CAPR). On the economic front, investors will be watching for the release of durable goods orders and the Dallas Fed manufacturing survey. On the earnings front, Dyne Therapeutics (DYNE), Applied Digital (APLD), and Navitas Semiconductor (NVTS) are among those reporting today. Shares of Sellas Life Sciences (SLS) climbed 1% premarket on Monday as investors weighed new big-money stake disclosures with the company nearing a potentially key Phase 3 catalyst for its acute myeloid leukemia (AML) drug. SLS stock fell 8% on Friday to $11.32, capping a 14% weekly decline and bringing its July loss to 23%. Quiver Quantitative data covering holdings as of June 30 showed a mix of buying and selling among recently reported institutional positions. Vision Financial Markets cut its stake by 294,600 shares, or 97%, leaving it with 9,800 shares valued at about $144,650. Martin Capital Advisors, meanwhile, disclosed a new 23,082-share position worth $340,690. EverSource Wealth Advisors added 9,942 shares, taking its holding to 10,039 shares valued at about $148,180. Additionally, Tradewinds Capital Management added 1,000 shares for a $14,760 position, while SignatureFD reduced its stake by 117 shares, or 68%, to 55 shares. Financial Consulate reported 600 shares, while Bogart Wealth disclosed two shares. The main focus for SLS investors is the Phase 3 Regal trial of galinpepimut-S, or GPS, in AML. The study has reached 78 of the 80 events required to trigger final analysis, putting Sellas within two events of one of the most important clinical readouts in its history. CEO Angelos Stergiou has previously called the slower-than-expected accumulation of events encouraging, given that the trial’s primary endpoint is tied to survival. Sellas has said RegalL would be considered successful if GPS extends median overall survival to 12.6 months versus 8 months with standard treatment. Stergiou also put Sellas’ broader oncology strategy in the spotlight during a Friday appearance on “FOX & Friends,” where he discussed the role of AI in matching cancer patients with treatments more likely to work for them. “What AI does, it can basically scan the lock and then design and select the right key for you,” Stergiou said, using a lock-and-key analogy to describe precision medicine. He also said that the company has used an early form of AI in work with Memorial Sloan Kettering and added that analyzing the genetic makeup of tumors could help speed drug development and improve patient selection. When asked whether AI could ultimately help beat cancer, Stergiou said he was “100% certain.” Retail investors continue to watch Sellas for signs of a potential partnership or acquisition. Stergiou fueled fresh speculation with a LinkedIn post thanking “collaborators, strategic partners, and shareholders” and saying he was “incredibly optimistic about the future.” Investors have also focused on updated change-of-control terms for senior executives. Under qualifying circumstances, CFO John Burns and Chief Development Officer Dragan Cicic would receive 15 months of base salary, target bonuses, COBRA coverage and full equity acceleration. (OTLK) rallied 12% overnight heading into Monday after the FDA approved Lytenava, the company’s eye drug for treating wet age-related macular degeneration (wet AMD), removing a major regulatory hurdle and putting the spotlight on how much value it can capture as it prepares for a U.S. launch. OTLK stock jumped 6% on Friday to $1.41, snapping two straight sessions of losses. Outlook Therapeutics said on Friday that the FDA approved Lytenava for wet AMD, making it the first and only FDA-approved version of Bevacizumab developed specifically for use in the eye. The decision came ahead of the FDA's July 29 target date and marks a major turnaround after several regulatory setbacks. In December 2025, the FDA rejected Outlook's application and asked for more evidence that the drug was effective. Outlook appealed, and in May the FDA's Office of New Drugs ruled that the existing data were sufficient and that no additional clinical trials were needed. That decision allowed Outlook to resubmit its application in June, leading to Friday's approval. Outlook estimates the U.S. market for anti-VEGF retinal treatments at about $8.5 billion annually, with millions of eye injections given each year. Bevacizumab has been used for more than 20 years in retinal care, including for wet AMD, but largely on an off-label basis. Lytenava stands out because it was developed specifically for injection into the eye and is now FDA-approved for wet AMD. Outlook also expects Lytenava to receive 12 years of U.S. market exclusivity under biologics law. The drug is already approved in the European Union and U.K., with commercial launches underway in Germany, Austria and the U.K. Outlook expects Lytenava to become available to eligible U.S. patients before year-end. Economist Paul Krugman warned that President Donald Trump's war against Iran has resulted in refining costs soaring, thereby magnifying the economic impact of higher crude prices. In a note published Thursday, the Nobel Prize-winning economist said crude oil prices hovering around $100 a barrel, combined with an unusually wide gasoline refining "crack spread" worth roughly another $40 per barrel, have left the world facing the economic equivalent of $140 per barrel for oil. “Trump’s gratuitous war on Iran has turned into a remarkable quagmire — remarkable because the only thing keeping the war going is Trump’s vanity. He effectively lost the war in the first few days,” Krugman said. The economist’s comments come amid an escalation in tensions between the U.S. and Iran. Trump said on Thursday that he will hold Iran responsible for any subsequent attacks by the Houthi rebels in the Red Sea, after an attack by the group on Saudi Arabian oil tankers in the region earlier this week. He also added that the U.S. will inflict “major military punishment” upon Iran and the Houthis if they attack ships again. Krugman argued that looking at crude oil prices alone understates the economic impact of the conflict. While benchmark crude has climbed to around $100 a barrel, he said the cost of turning crude into gasoline has also surged, with the refining "crack spread" widening to roughly $40 per barrel. Combined, those two components amount to the equivalent of $140 oil, according to Krugman. He said that the large refining margin means consumers are paying far more at the pump than crude prices alone would suggest, making the economic shock significantly more severe despite oil remaining well below historical peaks in nominal terms. The crack spread measures the difference between the price of crude oil and the value of refined products such as gasoline and diesel, serving as a key indicator of refinery profit margins. Crude oil prices eased on Friday after Brent soared past $100 a barrel on Thursday for the first time since May 20, 2026. U.S. West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude futures expiring in September were down 2.97%, hovering around $89.45 a barrel. Brent crude futures expiring in September fell 3.13%, hovering around $97.54 a barrel. The United States Oil Fund ETF (USO) and the ProShares Ultra Bloomberg Crude Oil ETF (UCO) were down about 2%. Krugman warned that the current energy shock could worsen significantly if the Iran conflict worsens. While he described the present situation as manageable, he said a broader regional war could disrupt energy supplies further and deepen the economic fallout. He also cautioned that any escalation would likely drive up both crude prices and refining margins, amplifying the pressure on consumers and businesses. "Things could get much uglier if this war escalates," Krugman wrote, arguing that the current equivalent of $140 oil may not represent the worst-case scenario. The economist argued that surging energy prices, combined with Trump's new tariffs, could reverse recent progress on inflation and push interest rates higher, intensifying the financial strain on households and businesses. This comes days ahead of the Federal Open Market Committee’s (FOMC) meeting later this month. title: Nasdaq Futures Lead US Premarket Rally As Iran Ceasefire Reports Ease Fears Ahead Of Big Tech Earnings: Why NVDA, ORCL, SPCX, XOM, OTLK Are In Focus - TradingView
content: U.S. stock futures surged early Monday after reports that the United States and Iran agreed to pause military strikes over the weekend triggered a sharp selloff in crude oil prices. Wall Street gears up for one of the busiest weeks this year, with nearly one-third of S&P 500 companies scheduled to report earnings, including four Magnificent Seven companies: Apple Inc. (AAPL), Amazon.com Inc. (AMZN), Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) and Meta Platforms Inc. (META). Investors will also be watching the Federal Reserve’s July policy decision, second-quarter GDP data and the Fed’s preferred inflation gauge, the PCE price index later this week. As of 4:00 a.m. ET, Nasdaq futures soared 1.5%, Dow and S&P 500 futures rose 0.9%, and Russell 2000 futures were up 1.2%. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment for the SPDR S&P 500 ETF (SPY), an exchange-traded fund that tracks the S&P 500 Index, remained ‘extremely bearish,’ while the Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ), which tracks the Nasdaq-100 Index, has moved to ‘bearish’ from ‘extremely bearish’ last week. Nvidia (NVDA): Rose 1% in early premarket trade after reports revealed it is in talks to provide a $250 billion financing backstop for OpenAI’s 10-gigawatt Ohio data center project. NVDA also announced a $500 billion partnership with SK Group, a $1B investment in South Korea's Naver, and the rollout of its first U.S.-made GB300 chips from TSMC’s Arizona fab. Oracle Corp. (ORCL): Shares saw a 3% relief rally in early premarket trade on Nvidia’s reported $250B OpenAI backstop. Since OpenAI is one of Oracle's largest cloud customers, traders viewed the development as a potential boost to Oracle’s long-term AI infrastructure business. Meanwhile, China's Moonshot AI is reportedly preparing to open-source its Kimi K3 model, renewing debate over whether Chinese AI developers are closing the gap with OpenAI and Anthropic. Alphabet Inc. (GOOGL): In focus after a top executive confirmed memory chip price hikes (up sixfold) will force higher pricing for the upcoming Pixel 11 series. SpaceX (SPCX): Shares were muted early premarket trade ahead of its Aug. 4 earnings report. Morningstar warned that upcoming post-IPO lockup expirations (Aug 6) could create selling pressure while simultaneously boosting the stock's float-adjusted weight inside the QQQ ETF. Outlook Therapeutics (OTLK): Shares rose 7% in early premarket trade following FDA approval of Lytenava for wet age-related macular degeneration (wet AMD), with analysts forecasting up to 290% upside. Oil stocks (USO, BATL, TPET, XOM, CVX, OXY) remained in focus as crude oil prices fell over 6% following the U.S.-Iran military pause. Other tickers trending on Stocktwits at the time of writing included Rigetti Computing (RGTI), Venture Global (VG) and Capricor Therapeutics (CAPR). On the economic front, investors will be watching for the release of durable goods orders and the Dallas Fed manufacturing survey. On the earnings front, Dyne Therapeutics (DYNE), Applied Digital (APLD), and Navitas Semiconductor (NVTS) are among those reporting today. title: 4 Energy Stocks With 20+ Years of Consecutive Dividend Growth - The Globe and Mail
content: The energy sector is known for its volatility, but it still contains some shockingly reliable dividend stocks. Chevron and ExxonMobil are two of the world's largest energy companies and two highly reliable dividend stocks. Enterprise Products Partners and Enbridge sidestep commodity risk and grow their dividends year after year. The geopolitical conflict in the Middle East has once again shown that energy prices are highly volatile. That's the norm for the sector, not the exception, a fact that can make it hard for dividend investors to find attractive energy stocks. But some companies have proven they have what it takes to keep paying through the entire energy cycle. If you are looking for reliable high-yield dividend stocks, Chevron(NYSE: CVX), ExxonMobil(NYSE: XOM), Enterprise Products Partners(NYSE: EPD), and Enbridge(NYSE: ENB) all deserve a deep dive. The shortest dividend streak on this list is 27 years! Where to invest $1,000 right now? Our analyst team just revealed what they believe are the 10 best stocks to buy right now, when you join Stock Advisor. See the stocks » Chevron and Exxon are two of the world's largest energy companies. They are also highly reliable dividend stocks, with decades worth of annual dividend increases behind each one. Exxon's streak is a bit longer at 43 years, but Chevron's 38-year streak is hard to complain about. Right now, Chevron has the higher yield at 3.7%, while Exxon still offers a well-above-market 2.7% yield. The big story here, however, is the businesses that back those yields and dividend streaks. Chevron and Exxon are both integrated energy companies, which means they provide investors exposure to the entire energy value chain, from the upstream (energy production) to the midstream (pipelines) to the downstream (chemical and refining). Their upstream operations have the biggest impact on financial results, but the midstream and downstream exposure helps to soften the large performance swings that often happen in the upstream. Meanwhile, both companies operate in a very conservative fiscal manner. That is highlighted by their peer-leading debt-to-equity ratios of 0.2x for Exxon and 0.25x for Chevron. This allows both companies to lean on their balance sheets during energy market downturns, enabling them to continue supporting their businesses and dividends. And that will allow dividend lovers to sleep well at night knowing that their dividend checks will keep rolling in. The upstream and the downstream are both volatile, but the midstream tends to be rather boring. This is where both Enterprise and Enbridge operate, each owning giant North American energy infrastructure systems. They charge fees for the use of their assets, so the price of the commodities being moved isn't all that important to their financial results. The benefit of this is clear in their dividend track records. Enterprise, a master limited partnership (MLP), has increased its distribution for 27 years, which is the shortest streak on this list, but basically as long as it has been public. Enbridge's dividend streak is 31 years in Canadian dollars. But what's really notable is their yields: Enterprise's is an ultra-high 5.7%, and Enbridge's is not far behind at 5%. There is one caveat here. The yields these midstream giants offer will likely make up a large portion of an investor's return over time. They are, at best, slow-growing and steady giants. Dividend hikes are likely to edge out inflation over time, but not by much. So these are most appropriate for investors looking to maximize the passive income they generate today. The on-again/off-again conflict in the Middle East has again shown that energy is a volatile sector. However, it has also shown how important energy is to the normal functioning of the global economy. Most investors should have some energy exposure in their portfolios. If you are a dividend lover, Chevron, Exxon, Enterprise, and Enbridge are four very strong options to consider given their impressive dividend histories. Your biggest decision will likely come down to how much direct energy exposure you are willing to take on. content: U.S. stock futures were lower early Monday amid the escalation of tensions in the Middle East following attacks by the United States and Israel on Iran. The strikes on Iran killed Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei on Saturday. Subsequent updates from the Israeli administration’s official channels, including its military and air force, highlighted the killings of several others in Iran’s political and intelligence apparatus. Iran’s ambassador to the International Atomic Energy Agency stated that the country’s nuclear site at Natanz has been hit in the U.S.-Israel strikes, according to a Reuters report. As of 5:30 a.m. ET on Monday, S&P futures traded 1% lower, Dow futures were down 1.1%, and Nasdaq futures declined 1.4%, while Russell 2000 futures lost 1.2%. Meanwhile, retail sentiment toward the SPDR S&P 500 ETF (SPY) has remained ‘bullish’, while the Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ) ETF, which tracks the Nasdaq 100 Index, has remained ‘neutral’. Crude oil prices rose to an eight-month high on Monday following the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. At the time of writing, U.S. West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude futures maturing in April were up 7.5% to $72 per barrel. Brent crude futures maturing in May gained 8% to $78.7 per barrel. Analysts at ING Think pointed out that while the U.S. has limited trade exposure to the Strait of Hormuz, its closure would fuel an increase in global oil prices, exacerbating the current cost-of-living crisis. “U.S. consumers are already stretched, and gasoline prices are acutely politically sensitive going into midterm territory. Higher oil prices would also complicate the Federal Reserve's future monetary policy path,” the firm stated in its latest note. (TSLA) shares fell about 4% in overnight trading heading into Monday after the company raised the price of its newly introduced entry-level Cybertruck, reversing a brief period when the electric pickup was offered at its lowest-ever starting price. Tesla launched its most affordable Cybertruck on Feb. 20 with a starting price of $59,990, positioning it below previous trims and closer to long-standing expectations of broader accessibility. However, effective March 1, the company increased the starting price to $69,990, marking a 17% jump and eliminating the temporary discount window that had lasted just 10 days. CEO Elon Musk had indicated at launch on X that the promotional pricing would be available only briefly, noting that the eventual price would depend on demand. The adjustment also returns the entry-level configuration to the same pricing level as the rear-wheel-drive version Tesla discontinued in September 2025. The company has also removed the lease option for the newly launched variant. With the latest revision, Tesla’s Cybertruck range resets across three tiers. The entry dual-motor all-wheel-drive (AWD) version now begins at $69,990, while the premium AWD trim remains priced at $79,990 and the tri-motor Cyberbeast sits at $99,990. When the Cybertruck was unveiled in 2019, Musk projected a starting price of about $39,990, with the most advanced configuration expected to begin near $70,000. When production finally began in November 2023, actual pricing entered the market well above those early projections. The lower-priced variant retains the same dual-motor powertrain and roughly 325-mile estimated range as the premium AWD model, but its original cost savings were achieved through a simplified interior and reduced feature set. Compared with higher trims, it substitutes textile seating for premium materials, pares back audio and comfort features, and replaces air suspension with coil springs, while also removing certain cabin technology elements. Cybertruck sales have so far fallen short of Tesla’s early ambitions. Around 20,000 units were sold in the U.S. last year, far below initial production targets. The company does not disclose Cybertruck deliveries separately; instead, it groups them within its “other models” category alongside the Model S and Model X. Despite this, updated ordering timelines now suggest delivery wait times stretching into 2027 for the entry AWD version in some U.S. regions. Alongside pricing adjustments, Tesla highlighted progress in its Full Self-Driving Supervised (FSD) system, which has now logged more than 8.4 billion cumulative miles, according to company data. Musk has previously said that roughly 10 billion miles of real-world driving data may be needed to support safe unsupervised autonomy at scale. During Tesla’s fourth-quarter earnings call, Musk also said the Cybertruck platform could be used for autonomous intra-city cargo delivery, calling it suitable for short-distance urban logistics if consumer demand for the vehicle falls short of expectations.
